question: According to the syllabus, how does an Old Testament prophet deliver the message he has received from God?

topic: Deuteronomy and the Former Prophets
question: What is meant by the “Deuteronomic” view of history?

options.text: The presentation of Israel’s history along the lines of Moses’ teaching in Deuteronomy, that obedience brings blessing and disobedience brings punishment
The view that history is governed by the fertility of the land rather than by God
options.rationale: That belongs to Baalism, not to Deuteronomy.

options.rationale: The syllabus says the Former Prophets are anonymous.

options.text: Achan coveted some of the spoils from Jericho and kept them for himself instead of offering them all to God

His one failure was

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: What period does the book of Judges cover?

options.text: Between the exodus and the entry into Canaan, roughly 1290 to 1220 B.C.
options.rationale: That period belongs to the Law and to the opening of Joshua.

options.text: Between the rise of Samuel and the death of David, roughly 1075 to 975 B.C.
options.rationale: That is the period covered by the books of Samuel.

options.text: Between the death of Solomon and the fall of Samaria, roughly 930 to 722 B.C.
options.rationale: That period is covered by the books of Kings.

options.text: Between Joshua’s death and the rise of Samuel, roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C.

explanation: Judges describes a time of transition in which the only thing holding the scattered tribes together was their common faith.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
manualReference.excerpt:
Judges covers the period in Israel's history between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel - 
roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Brief Survey of the Former Prophets

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: Judges 17:6 and 21:25 explain the moral chaos of the period by saying: “There was no ______ in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes.”
explanation: The absence of a king is the book’s own explanation for the moral and religious decline recorded in its closing chapters.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
manualReference.excerpt:
In Judges 17:6 and 21:25, the explanation given for this state of affairs is that, "There was no 
King in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes".
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Brief Survey of the Former Prophets

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: What does the syllabus say about the division of I and II Samuel into two books?

options.text: They were always two separate scrolls in the Hebrew Old Testament
options.rationale: The syllabus states the opposite.

options.text: They were divided by the compilers of the English Bible
options.rationale: The division goes back to the Septuagint, as with Kings.

options.text: They were divided into two by Samuel himself
options.rationale: Samuel is not the writer; he is the dominating figure after whom the books are named.

options.text: They were originally one volume in the Hebrew Old Testament and were divided into two by the Septuagint (LXX)

explanation: The same is said of Kings: originally one volume, divided into two at the time of the Septuagint.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
manualReference.excerpt:
I & II Samuel were originally one volume, or one book as contained in the Hebrew Old 
Testament. It was the Septuagint (LXX) that divided it into two.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Brief Survey of the Former Prophets

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: The books of Samuel bear his name because he wrote them.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The syllabus says the name is given because Samuel is the dominating figure and the king maker who anointed both Saul and David, not because he was the writer.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
manualReference.excerpt:
The name Samuel is given to the books not because he is the writer, but because he is 
the dominating figure. He is seen in the book as the King maker - he anointed both Saul and 
David as Kings.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Brief Survey of the Former Prophets

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: The books of Kings cover four centuries of Israel’s history. In which years did Samaria fall and Jerusalem suffer destruction?

options.text: Samaria fell in 746 B.C. and Jerusalem was destroyed in 561 B.C.
options.rationale: 746 B.C. is the end of Jeroboam II’s reign, and 561 B.C. is connected with the release of Jehoiachin.

options.text: Samaria fell in 930 B.C. and Jerusalem was destroyed in 722 B.C.
options.rationale: 930 B.C. is the close of David’s reign, at which the books of Kings begin.

options.text: Samaria fell in 722 B.C. and Jerusalem was destroyed in 587 B.C.
Samaria fell in 587 B.C. and Jerusalem was destroyed in 722 B.C.
options.rationale: The dates are the wrong way round.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
manualReference.excerpt:
The two books cover four centuries (400 years) of 
Israel's history from the close of David's reign (930 B.C) through the golden age of 
Solomon, and the rift between Israel and Judah, to the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and the 
destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BC
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Brief Survey of the Former Prophets

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: Besides the reign of Solomon, what is the other great interest of the books of Kings?

options.text: The conquest and division of the Promised Land
options.rationale: That is the subject of Joshua.

options.text: The priestly ordinances of the temple, as in Chronicles
options.rationale: The syllabus contrasts Kings with the priestly volumes of Chronicles.

options.text: The prophetic ministry of Elijah and Elisha, the northern “resistance” movement against Ahab and the Baal religion of Jezebel
The ministry of Samuel as judge and king maker
options.rationale: That belongs to the books of Samuel.

explanation: Their revolt was marked by power to work miracles, which had not been seen in Israel since the exodus.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
manualReference.excerpt:
The other great interest of Kings is the prophetic ministry of Elijah and Elisha. They 
represented the great northern "resistance" movement against the corrupting influence 
of King Ahab and the Baal religion of his wife Jezebel.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Brief Survey of the Former Prophets

question: Where did the prophet Elijah come from, and in whose reign did he prophesy?

options.text: From Tishbe in Gilead, during the reign of Ahab (c. 873–851 B.C.)
From Bethel in Israel, during the reign of Jehoahaz

options.text: From Samaria, during the reign of Jehoash

the Prophet Elijah, who came 
from Tishbe in Gilead prophesied during the reign of Ahab (c. 873 -851 B.C.), while Elisha's

manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY — Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan

subject: OT
chapter: PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY
topic: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
question: What theological position does the syllabus assign to Yahwism, the Israelite religion?

options.text: Atheism — no god could be represented or named
options.rationale: Yahwism abhorred visual representation, but it was emphatically the worship of Yahweh.

options.text: Pantheism — the land itself was divine
options.rationale: Baalism was the religion tied to the land; Yahwism laid no stress on sacred places.

options.text: Polytheism — many gods were to be worshipped together
options.rationale: It is Baalism that the syllabus calls a polytheistic religion.

options.text: Monolatry or henotheism — worship was to be given exclusively to Yahweh

explanation: Yahwism laid no stress on sanctuaries or sacred places, allowed no statues or pictures, and laid strong emphasis on morality and the keeping of the commandments given at Sinai.

manualReference.topicTitle: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
manualReference.chapterTitle: PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY
manualReference.excerpt:
Yahwism, the Israelite religion, has a theological position of monolatry or henotheism, (i.e. 
worship was to be given exclusively to Yahweh). It abhors visual representation of any kind.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY — Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan

subject: OT
chapter: PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY
topic: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
question: Which of the following does the syllabus give as features of Baalism? Select all that apply.

options.text: It laid great emphasis on local shrines, sanctuaries and high places
It abhorred visual representation of any kind
options.rationale: That is a mark of Yahwism, not of Baalism.

options.text: It laid strong emphasis on morality and the keeping of the commandments
options.rationale: The syllabus says Baalism laid no stress at all on morality.

options.text: It was purely an agricultural religion
It was a religion tied to the land, of times and seasons

explanation: Baalism was intimately connected with the fertility of the land: to worship Baal was to celebrate rites and festivals designed to procure that fertility.

manualReference.topicTitle: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
manualReference.chapterTitle: PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY
manualReference.excerpt:
Baalism, by contrast, was a religion tied to the land, a religion of times and seasons. It was 
purely an agricultural religion that laid great emphasis on local shrines, sanctuaries, and high places.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY — Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan

chapter: PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY

options.text: They are set entirely in the Southern Kingdom of Judah
options.rationale: Both Elijah and Elisha exercised their ministry in the North.

options.text: They are concerned wholly with the royal court and the guidance of kings
options.rationale: Guiding the king was the special responsibility of the court prophets.

options.text: They do not show the same tension between Yahwism and Baalism, but the performance of signs and wonders at personal and national levels

Elisha's traditions, however, do not show the same tension between Yahwism and Baalisrn,

question: Where was Tekoa, the home town of the prophet Amos?

options.text: A settlement by the Dead Sea where the sycamore fig trees grew

options.text: A village in the Northern Kingdom, about twelve miles from Samaria
options.rationale: Amos came from the Southern Kingdom of Judah, though he was sent to preach in the North.

A priestly city attached to the sanctuary at Bethel

Amos was from a town called Tekoa, a small mountain-top town in Judah, (Amos

topic: The Prophet Amos

manualReference.topicTitle: The Prophet Amos

Two terms are used to describe Amos (in Amos 7:14) a Shepherd and a 
dresser of sycamore fig-trees.

topic: The Historical Background to Amos' Ministry
question: During whose reign did Amos deliver his message, and what were the years of that reign?

options.text: Uzziah, king of Judah

options.text: Jeroboam II, who ruled Israel from 786 to 746 B.C.

topic: The Ministry of Amos
question: What did Amos mean when he told Amaziah, “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet’s son”?

options.rationale: Amos was answering Amaziah’s challenge by explaining how he became a prophet.

topic: The Ministry of Amos

topic: The Ministry of Amos

subject: OT

options.text: They prove that Amos had travelled widely among the nations
options.rationale: The syllabus says nothing of such travels; his migrant work took him only into the North.

options.text: They show that Israel alone stood under God’s authority
options.rationale: The syllabus says all nations and all people stand under his authority.

options.text: They show that the surrounding nations were more wicked than Israel
options.rationale: Israel itself is the climax of the series and receives the fullest indictment.

options.text: They indicate Yahweh’s sovereignty beyond his covenant people: he is King of his world and judges sin wherever it occurs

explanation: Each oracle follows the same structure — messenger formula, offence, punishment, concluding messenger formula — and together they display God as ruler of all nations.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
manualReference.excerpt:
The significance of the prophecy against the nations is to indicate the concept of Yahweh's 
sovereignty beyond His covenant people. God is portrayed as the King of His world who 
judges sin and unrighteousness irrespective of where it may occur.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: In the oracle against Syria, where were many Syrians to be carried?

options.text: To Kir, the land of their former slavery, located in Mesopotamia
To Edom, to be sold as slaves
options.rationale: It was Philistia and Tyre that sold Israelites into slavery to Edom.

options.text: To Damascus, the capital city
options.rationale: Damascus was Syria’s own capital, whose palace God would burn down.

options.text: To Kirioth, the capital of Moab
options.rationale: Kirioth was Moab’s capital, not a place of Syrian exile.

explanation: Syria’s offence was that it had often harassed Israel, especially under Ben-Hadad and King Hazael; its punishment included burning of the palace, breaking of strongholds and deportation to Kir.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
manualReference.excerpt: Cause many Syrians to die and others to be carried back into Kir, the land of their former slavery, (2 Kings 16:9). Kir was located in Mesopotamia
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: The offence charged against Ammon was that its people ripped open pregnant Israelite women with swords during their wars of expansion in Gilead.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Ammonites were descendants of Lot’s youngest daughter; their punishment was that their cities would be destroyed and the inhabitants enslaved.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
manualReference.excerpt:
The Ammonites, who were descendants of Lot's youngest daughter (Gen. 19: 36-38) had committed serious crimes against Israel. They ripped open pregnant 
Israelite women with swords during their wars of expansion in Gilead.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: In the oracle against Israel (Amos 2:6–16), which of the following are named among the offences? Select all that apply.

options.text: They sold the poor into slavery, trading them for a pair of shoes
They perverted justice by accepting bribes
Both fathers and sons were guilty of immorality with the same harlot
They broke a covenant of brotherhood made with Israel
options.rationale: That was the offence charged against Phoenicia, whose capital was Tyre.

options.text: They desecrated the tombs of the kings of Edom
options.rationale: That was the offence charged against Moab.

explanation: Israel, with its capital Samaria, is the eighth and climactic oracle: the nation that had received most from God is charged with the fullest catalogue of sin.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
manualReference.excerpt:
They had perverted justice by accepting bribes, sold the poor into slavery, 
trading them for a pair of shoes, both fathers and sons were guilty of immorality with the same harlot, and lounging in stolen clothing from their debtors at religious feasts.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: In the vision of the plumb line God said he would destroy the dynasty of Jeroboam II by the sword. How does the syllabus say this came about?

options.text: Jeroboam II himself was killed in battle at Ramoth-Gilead
options.rationale: It was Ahab who died in the battle at Ramoth-Gilead.

options.text: Jeroboam II was succeeded by his son Zechariah, who was assassinated after a reign of only six months
His household was carried captive to Kir
options.rationale: Kir was the place of exile named in the oracle against Syria.

options.text: Samaria fell to the Assyrians within a year of the vision
options.rationale: Samaria fell in 722 B.C., some years after Jeroboam’s dynasty ended.

explanation: God told Amos he would continue to test Israel with the plumb line of heavenly justice, and would no longer turn away from punishing them; the same plumb line was later used on Judah under Manasseh.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
manualReference.excerpt:
Jeroboam II was 
succeeded by his son Zechariah, who was assassinated by a rebel named Shall urn after a reign of only six months (2 Kings 15:10-12).
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: What did the basket of ripe summer fruit symbolise in the fourth of Amos’s visions?

options.text: The restoration of agriculture in the last days
options.rationale: The restoration of agriculture is promised at Amos 9:13, not in this vision.

options.text: The offerings the merchants brought to the shrine at Bethel
options.rationale: The vision concerns judgment on the merchants, not their offerings.

options.text: Israel, which was now ripe for judgment
The abundance of the reign of Jeroboam II
options.rationale: The prosperity of the reign is background to the book, not the meaning of the vision.

explanation: The vision goes on to charge the merchants with robbing the poor, longing for the Sabbath to end, and making slaves of the poor for a piece of silver or a pair of shoes.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
manualReference.excerpt:
The Lord showed Amos a basket 
filled with ripe fruit. He then explained to Amos that it symbolized Israel which was now 
ripe for judgment.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: What was the outcome of the first vision, the plague of locusts?

options.text: The vision was withheld from Israel and told only to Amaziah
options.rationale: Amaziah appears in the account of Amos’s call, not here.

options.text: Amos interceded for Israel and the destruction did not take place
Amos was forbidden to intercede for the people
options.rationale: Intercession is named in the syllabus as one of the roles of the prophets, and Amos exercised it here.

options.text: The locusts destroyed the crops as the vision had shown
options.rationale: The syllabus says the destruction did not take place because Amos interceded.

explanation: The same happened with the second vision, the destructive fire: the prophet pleaded for mercy and God set the deserved punishment aside.

manualReference.topicTitle: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
manualReference.excerpt:
God revealed to Amos in a vision that the crops were to be 
destroyed by an invasion of locusts. Amos interceded for Israel and the destruction did 
not take place.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

subject: OT
topic: Conclusion
question: How does Amos describe the restoration with which his prophecy closes?

options.text: As permanent — Israel would be planted in their own land, never again to be uprooted
As temporary, lasting only until the exile
options.rationale: The syllabus stresses that the restoration would be permanent.

options.text: As limited to the tribe of Judah
options.rationale: The promise is of the restoration of the people of Israel scattered throughout the world.

options.text: As conditional upon the repentance of Jeroboam II
options.rationale: The oracles offered no hope for the future to Jeroboam’s Israel; the restoration lies beyond judgment.

explanation: Amos began with judgment and doom to show that God is just, and ends with a permanent restoration, showing how God delights to bless his people and to welcome the repentant sinner.

manualReference.topicTitle: Conclusion
manualReference.excerpt:
He states 
finally that this Restoration would be permanent (9: 15), "I will plant Israel in their own land, 
never again to be uprooted from the land I have given them" says the Lord your God.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Conclusion

subject: OT
topic: INTRODUCTION
question: What place does the Book of Malachi occupy in the Hebrew canon of the Old Testament?

options.text: It stands among the Writings, the third division of the Hebrew canon
options.rationale: Malachi belongs to the Prophets, not to the Writings.

options.text: It is a post-exilic prophetic book which concludes the prophetic books of the Hebrew canon
It opens the collection known as “The Twelve” or the Minor Prophets
options.rationale: Malachi is one of the Twelve, but it closes rather than opens the prophetic books.

options.text: It is the last of the Former Prophets
options.rationale: The Former Prophets are Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings.

explanation: The book speaks of the love of God and of the obedience by which our love for him is shown, and it concludes the prophetic books of the Hebrew canon.

manualReference.topicTitle: INTRODUCTION
manualReference.excerpt:
The Book of Malachi is one of the post exilic prophetic books which concludes the prophetic 
books of the Hebrew canon of the Old Testament. It is one of the shortest books which make 
up "The Twelve" or the Minor Prophets.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — INTRODUCTION

subject: OT
topic: INTRODUCTION
question: The Book of Malachi is closely linked with the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, and from them the post-exilic period of Jewish history is better understood.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The three post-exilic prophets belong together, and Malachi’s setting can only be fixed by reference to the ministries of Haggai and Zechariah.

manualReference.topicTitle: INTRODUCTION
manualReference.excerpt:
The Book of Malachi is closely linked with the prophets Haggai and Zechariah and from them 
we get to understand better, the post exilic period of the Jewish History.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — INTRODUCTION

subject: OT
topic: The Prophet Malachi
question: What does the name Malachi mean?

options.text: “My Messenger”
“Oracle”
options.rationale: Massa, the Hebrew word for oracle, means a burden laid upon the messenger.

options.text: “My Servant”
options.rationale: The syllabus gives “My Messenger” as the meaning of the name.

options.text: “Burden-bearer”
options.rationale: That is the meaning of the name Amos.

explanation: Whether the word is his personal name or a title of his office, Malachi was a communicator of God’s word whose message was full of rebuke, but intended to turn the people back to God.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Prophet Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: His Name: The name MALACHI means "My Messenger".
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The Prophet Malachi

subject: OT
topic: The Prophet Malachi
question: Nothing is known of Malachi’s personal history: neither the names of his parents nor his home are given in his book or in Ezra and Nehemiah.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The book tells us nothing of the man himself, which is one reason some scholars have argued that “Malachi” is a title rather than a personal name.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Prophet Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: There is nothing in the book of Malachi or the Historical books of Ezra and Nehemiah about his personal history. The names of his parents and his home are not known.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The Prophet Malachi

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
question: What is the first indication given that Malachi prophesied after the return from the Babylonian exile?

options.text: He mentions a “governor” as being over the land (1:8), whereas before the exile the political leader was a king
He refers to the rebuilding of the temple as still in progress
options.rationale: There is no reference to the rebuilding of the temple; that silence is itself part of the argument.

options.text: He names Nehemiah as the governor of Judah
options.rationale: Malachi does not name the governor; the link with Nehemiah rests on the agreement between Nehemiah 13 and the book.

options.text: He speaks of the four hundred years of silence to follow
options.rationale: The four hundred years of silence is a later reckoning, not a statement of the book.

explanation: A governor over the land was the political condition that existed when the Jews returned from Babylon; Haggai used the same word of Zerubbabel.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Ministry of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
First, the Prophet must have prophesied after the exile because he mentions a "governor" as being over the land (1:8). This was a political condition which existed when the Jews 
returned from Babylon. Before the exile, the political leader of the nation was a "Kinq".
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The Ministry of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
question: During which years does the syllabus say Haggai and Zechariah prophesied?

options.text: During the exile itself, 587–539 B.C.
options.rationale: Haggai and Zechariah prophesied after the return, at the rebuilding of the temple.

options.text: During the governorship of Nehemiah, 445–433 B.C.
options.rationale: Those are the dates of Nehemiah’s governorship, to which Malachi himself is linked.

options.text: During the reign of Jeroboam II, 786–746 B.C.
options.rationale: That is the setting of the ministry of Amos.

options.text: During the building of the temple, 520–516 B.C.

explanation: Malachi must be later still, since the temple services had been resumed long enough for the priests to grow weary of them and for irregularities to creep in.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Ministry of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
he must have prophesied after the ministry of Haggai and Zechariah who prophesied 
during the time of the building of the temple (520 - 516 B.C.).
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The Ministry of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
question: When did Nehemiah come to Jerusalem as governor, and when did he return temporarily to Persia?

options.text: He came in 445 B.C. and returned to Persia in 433 B.C.
He came in 516 B.C. and returned to Persia in 500 B.C.
options.rationale: The syllabus gives 445 B.C. and 433 B.C.

options.text: He came in 520 B.C. and returned to Persia in 516 B.C.
options.rationale: Those are the years of the building of the temple under Haggai and Zechariah.

options.text: He came in 433 B.C. and returned to Persia in 420 B.C.
options.rationale: 433 B.C. is the year of his temporary return to Persia, not of his arrival.

explanation: On his return to Jerusalem Nehemiah found gross sin and violation of the Law, and the close agreement between Nehemiah 13 and Malachi suggests the prophet worked a few years after 433 B.C.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Ministry of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
Nehemiah came to Jerusalem to be governor in 445 Be. He served in that capacity for some 
years and then returned temporarily to Persia in 433 B.C. (Nehemiah 5:14).
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The Ministry of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
question: Malachi is the last prophet of the Old Testament; his book is followed by ______ years of silence, after which John the Baptist appeared to prepare the way for the Messiah.
explanation: The book ends the Old Testament revelation, and the syllabus reckons four hundred silent years between Malachi and John the Baptist.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Ministry of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
There is then the four hundred years of silence after which the Prophet John the 
Baptist appeared on the scene to "prepare the way" for the Messiah the Lord Jesus Christ.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The Ministry of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: The nature of His Message
question: What recurring literary method is a common feature of the Book of Malachi?

options.text: A vision described and then interpreted by an angel
options.rationale: Visions of that kind belong to other prophets; Malachi works by charge and reply.

options.text: A charge against Israel, followed by an objection in the form of a question put into the mouth of the hearers, which is then answered
A parable followed by a prayer of confession
options.rationale: The syllabus describes no such pattern in Malachi.

options.text: An oracle against a foreign nation followed by one against Israel
options.rationale: That is the pattern of Amos 1:3–2:16.

explanation: The words placed in the mouth of the Lord’s opponents represent the attitudes and actions of the people as the prophet understood them, and are meant to show the Israelites their true selves.

manualReference.topicTitle: The nature of His Message
manualReference.excerpt:
Charges or accusations are made against Israel, which is usually an opening statement 
(e.g.: "I have loved you" says the Lord 1:2). These are then followed by objections on the part 
of the accused (in the form of a question) put into the mouth of the hearers
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The nature of His Message

subject: OT
topic: The nature of His Message
question: Complete the theme of the Book of Malachi: “God’s Rebuke of Israel’s ______ Sins”.
explanation: The theme is developed into six charges against the nation, from doubting God’s love to discrediting God’s service.

manualReference.topicTitle: The nature of His Message
manualReference.excerpt: The theme of the Book of Malachi is "God's Rebuke of Israel's Outrageous Sins".
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The nature of His Message

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: What does the Hebrew word for oracle, Massa, mean as it is used in Malachi?

options.text: A covenant of brotherhood between two nations
options.rationale: That phrase belongs to the oracle against Tyre in Amos.

options.text: A vision granted to a seer
options.rationale: Vision belongs to the words rõ’eh and hõzeh, not to Massa.

options.text: A “burden” imposed by a master, a ruler or a deity on his subjects
A tenth part set aside for God
options.rationale: A tenth is the meaning of ma’aser, the Hebrew word for tithe.

explanation: The messenger would not have chosen to say such a thing: the burden has been laid on his heart by the Lord and he is obliged to discharge it.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
The 
word "Oracle" as used in Malachi means a "burden" imposed by a master or a ruler or a deity 
on his subjects.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: How does the syllabus explain the words “Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated”?

options.text: They describe the personal characters of the two brothers
options.rationale: The contrast is between two nations, Israel and Edom, not two temperaments.

options.text: The terms loved and hated are to be explained as preference, not animosity
They show God rejecting the covenant he made with the fathers
options.rationale: The covenant with the fathers stands; Israel’s very existence is offered as proof of God’s love.

options.text: They are a prediction of the future conversion of Edom
options.rationale: The syllabus points instead to Edom’s destruction as a nation.

explanation: God answers the complaint “How have you loved us?” by pointing Israel to its own history: its continued existence as a nation, set against Edom which was a nation no longer.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: The terms LOVED and HATED could be explained as preference, not animosity.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: How, according to Malachi, had the priests despised God’s name?

options.text: By placing defiled, ritually unclean food upon his altar, offering blind, crippled or diseased animals
By refusing to serve at the altar at all
options.rationale: The problem was careless service, not the abandonment of service.

options.text: By keeping back the tithes and offerings
options.rationale: That was the separate charge that Israel had disregarded God’s tithes.

options.text: By marrying the daughters of a strange god
options.rationale: That was the charge that Israel had defied God’s law on marriage.

explanation: The Law of Moses required that only the best animals be brought to God’s altar; by bringing the sick, the blind and the lame they were saying in effect, “You are unworthy of our best.”

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: How have the priests despised God's name? By placing defiled (ritually unclean) food upon His altar.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: Malachi’s condemnation of mixed marriages rests on religious rather than racial or ethnic grounds.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The men of Israel had married the daughters of a strange god — heathen women who were idolaters — and God had prohibited such marriages because they would lead Israel into idolatry.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
This is an issue of 
religion. It is marrying people of other Faith which is being condemned and not because 
of ethnicity.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: Why does Malachi treat the divorcing of a wife as an act of cruelty?

options.text: Because it left the children of the marriage without a name
options.rationale: The children appear under a different head — divorce frustrates God’s design for a godly seed.

options.text: Because it profaned the covenant God made with the fathers
options.rationale: That is God’s evaluation of intermarriage with idolaters in 2:10-11.

options.text: Because it is not merely the putting away of a woman, but of a woman who is “his companion”, who has shared her life and life’s experiences with him
Because the divorced wife had no legal means of support
options.rationale: The syllabus rests the charge on the relationship betrayed, not on economics.

explanation: The syllabus sets out four things about divorce: it is an act of cruelty, an act of disloyalty, an act which frustrates God’s design for a godly seed, and an act which God hates.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: Divorcing one's wife was an act of cruelty because it was not merely the putting away of a woman, but the putting away of a woman who is "HIS COMPANION. . ."
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: In Malachi 2:16 God states clearly, “I ______ divorce.”
explanation: It was bad enough that the men of Israel entered mixed marriages; worse still that they were divorcing their Jewish wives in order to do so.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: Here, God states clearly "I HATE DIVORCE" (v16).
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: With what problem did the Jews of Malachi’s day struggle, so that they disdained God’s justice?

options.text: Why the exile had lasted seventy years
options.rationale: The book addresses the community after the return, not the length of the exile.

options.text: Why God had chosen Jacob rather than Esau
options.rationale: That question belongs to the first charge, that Israel had doubted God’s love.

options.text: Why the temple had not yet been rebuilt
options.rationale: The temple had already been rebuilt; the silence about it is one argument for a late date.

options.text: Why the wicked apparently prosper while the righteous suffer

explanation: Their complaint was, “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord … or where is the God of justice?” — a view that leaves out God’s long-suffering and his own timetable for judgment.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: the Jews of Malachi's day continued to struggle with the problem of why the wicked apparently prosper while the righteous suffer.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: What is the Hebrew word for tithe, and what does it mean?

options.text: Massa, meaning a “burden”
options.rationale: Massa is the Hebrew word for oracle.

options.text: Ma’aser, meaning a “tenth”
Hevel, meaning a “band”
options.rationale: Hevel is the word used of the bands of prophets.

options.text: Nõqĕd, meaning a “sheep owner”
options.rationale: Nõqĕd is the term used of Amos in Amos 1:1.

explanation: The practice is very old: it was known in Babylon, Persia, Egypt and China, and Abraham knew of it when he migrated from Ur.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: The Hebrew word for Tithe is, ma'aser, and it means a 'Tenth'.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: Under the Levitical system a penalty of twenty percent of the tithe was exacted from anyone who sold his tithes and refused to use the money to pay for a substitute.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Leviticus 27:30 makes it clear that a tithe of everything belonged to the Lord and was holy to him; when the Levites received the tithe they in turn gave a tenth for the priests.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
A penalty of twenty percent of the tithe was exacted 
from anyone who sold his tithes and refused to use the money to pay for a substitute
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: What does Malachi tell the people to do about their disregard of the tithes, and what does God promise in return?

options.text: They must pay a further twenty percent as a penalty
options.rationale: The twenty per cent penalty belonged to the earlier Levitical provision, not to Malachi’s call.

options.text: They must repent and bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, and God will open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing
They must sell their tithes and bring the money to the priests instead
options.rationale: That permission belonged to Hebrews living far from the temple, and it led to gross abuses.

options.text: They must ask the Levites to pay the tithe on their behalf
options.rationale: The Levites received the tithe; they did not pay it for the people.

explanation: By withholding the tithes the people were robbing God, and were already experiencing his chastisement; repentance would bring the removal of that chastisement from their agriculture.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt:
They must repent and "bring the whole tithe 
into the store house," If they are willing to do this, God will open the windows of heaven, 
and pour out a blessing on them.
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: Three things are said about the godly remnant in Malachi 3:16. Select the three.

options.text: They spoke to one another, defending God’s actions and exhorting one another not to lose heart
They brought only the best animals to the altar
options.rationale: The Law required the best animals, but this is not among the three things said of the remnant.

options.text: They feared or reverenced the Lord and served him faithfully
They esteemed his name
They complained that it was vain to serve God
options.rationale: That was the complaint of the majority, who by it discredited God’s service.

explanation: The remnant stands in contrast to the rest of the nation, who by their lifestyle showed that they despised God’s name; of the godly a book of remembrance was written before the Lord.

manualReference.topicTitle: Outline of the Book of Malachi
manualReference.excerpt: Three things are said about the godly: (1) They feared (or reverenced) the Lord and served Him faithfully; (2) they spoke to one another - defending God's actions, and exhorting one another not to lose heart in spite of their hard conditions of life; and (3) they esteemed his name
manualReference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi

subject: OT
topic: Conclusion: (Read Malachi 4:4-6)
question: What is the admonition with which the Book of Malachi closes (4:4)?

options.text: That Israel should remember the law of Moses, the decrees and laws commanded him at Horeb for all Israel
That Israel should rebuild the temple without delay
options.rationale: The temple had long been rebuilt by Malachi’s day.

options.text: That Israel should bring the whole tithe into the storehouse
options.rationale: That call belongs to the charge concerning the tithes in 3:7-12.

options.text: That Israel should put away the daughters of a strange god
options.rationale: The charge concerning mixed marriage stands at 2:10-16.

subject: OT

topic: Who is a Prophet?
question: Explain who a prophet is in the Old Testament, with particular reference to the three Hebrew words used to designate the prophets.
idealAnswer: In the Old Testament three Hebrew words are normally used to designate the prophets: Nāvi, rõ'eh and hõzeh. Rõ'eh and hõzeh are properly rendered "seer" and are practically synonymous in meaning. Nāvi, on the other hand, is difficult to explain etymologically, that is, by tracing the root word or the origin and history of the word; its meaning can only be worked out by looking at the way it is used. Each of the three words designates one who is a spokesman for God. The use of Nāvi may be seen in Exodus 4:15-16, where Aaron is to be Moses' spokesman to the people, and in Exodus 7:1, where the Lord tells Moses that he has been made like God to Pharaoh and that Aaron will be his prophet. In these passages Moses stood in relation to Pharaoh as God, and between them was Aaron who was to speak to Pharaoh on behalf of Moses; Aaron was a Nāvi. The man who can be designated a Nāvi, then, is one who speaks forth for God. Rõ'eh and hõzeh primarily refer to the fact that the person so designated sees the message God gives him or her. This seeing may mean that the message first comes through a vision, and in some instances it did; but although the two words may refer to sight, they usually refer to insight. Thus the words rõ'eh and hõzeh designate one who, whether by vision or otherwise, is given insight into the mind of God, and who declares what has been seen as a message to the people. A prophet in the Old Testament, therefore, is a person who receives a message from God and utters the actual words that God has given to him, without any modification or interpretation on his part. This is illustrated in Deuteronomy 18:18: "I will put my words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him." In the Old Testament the prophets are also given various other names, including man of God, seer, soothsayer and fortune-teller.

subject: OT
chapter: INTRODUCTION TO PROPHETS AND PROPHECY IN ISRAEL
topic: The Establishment of the Prophetic Institution
question: Give an account of the establishment of the prophetic institution in Israel.
idealAnswer: The prophetic institution became necessary during the settlement of the nation of Israel in the Promised Land. When Israel entered Canaan they had the Law as a precious possession. This Law, revealed by God at Mount Sinai, laid the broad basis on which the life of the people of God was to be built and guided: the Ten Commandments were seen as the basis of the principles of ethics and morality, while other rules for particular situations were expressed in the other laws. The Law, however, was not adequate to meet all the situations that would arise when they settled in the Promised Land. This inadequacy was not due to any inherent weakness in the Law itself, but simply to the fact that the Law did not speak in detail on every possible situation that would arise in Israel's life. There would be occasions when a specific revelation of God would be needed to show the nation the course it should pursue, and that revelation God would give through his servants the prophets. Again, when Israel entered Canaan the people of that land sought to learn about the future and the will of the gods by means the Bible calls "abominations" or "detestable ways" (Deuteronomy 18:9). There was the danger that the Israelites would be influenced by the Canaanites and learn to do the same; and to avoid this danger the Lord declared that he would raise up prophets whom the Israelites were to hear and obey. The prophets whom the Lord would raise up were to be like Moses. Just as Moses was a mediator between God and the nation, so the prophets would serve as mediators; and just as the priests represented the people before God, so the prophets represented God to the people. In ancient Greece and in the Mesopotamian countries there were the god, the oracle, the prophet and the people, but in Israel there was only one intermediary between God and the people, and this arrangement was truly unique. One who heard the words of the prophet heard the very words of God himself, and these words required implicit obedience. According to the testimony of the Bible, the prophetic institution of Israel was of divine origin: God himself set it up (Deuteronomy 18:15-18).

chapter: INTRODUCTION TO PROPHETS AND PROPHECY IN ISRAEL
topic: Facts about Prophecy in Israel
question: Discuss the tests by which the people of Israel could distinguish between true and false prophets.
idealAnswer: In every religion there are true and false prophets, and Israel's true religion had always been plagued by imitators alongside the faithful and true prophets of the Lord. There were men who had not received a revelation from God but who claimed to have received messages from him; Jeremiah refused to have anything to do with such men. In the Old Testament there were three tests which the people could use to discern between true and false prophets. The first is the theological test (Deuteronomy 13). Through Moses there had been a revelation of the Lord who brought his people out of Egypt; therefore, even if a prophet performed some signs to give validation to what he was saying, if his message contradicted Mosaic theology — the truth known about the Lord who brought his people out of Egypt — the prophet was false. The second is the practical test (Deuteronomy 18:20ff): the prophecy that is not fulfilled has not come from the Lord. It must be noted that this is a negative test. It does not say that fulfilment is proof that the Lord has spoken, since fulfilment might in fact be offered as evidence by a false prophet to validate his word; what is not fulfilled is not from the Lord. The third is the moral test (Jeremiah 23:9ff). This is a test to be applied first to the lives of the prophets themselves and then to the tendency of the message they preached. Do they strengthen the hands of evildoers, assuring them that they need not fear the judgment to come? That is a sure sign that they have not stood before the Lord to hear his word. The prophet who comes fresh from the Lord's presence has a message turning people from evil. The syllabus illustrates these tests from 1 Kings 22, where four hundred false prophets encouraged Ahab and Jehoshaphat to fight at Ramoth-Gilead and only Micaiah son of Imlah discouraged them; Micaiah's words proved true and Ahab died in battle. Often the false prophets were greater in number and more popular, telling the king what he wanted to hear and making no moral demands. Above all, they had not stood in the council of the Lord.

subject: OT
topic: Deuteronomy and the Former Prophets
question: Explain what is meant by the "Deuteronomic" view of history, and show how it is reflected in the Former Prophets.
idealAnswer: When we read the story of the call of Moses in Exodus 4:14-17 we note that Aaron was to be Moses' Nabi, that is, Aaron was to speak on behalf of Moses; in short, a prophet speaks on behalf of another person or of a deity. In the Book of Deuteronomy there are several passages depicting Moses speaking on behalf of God to the people of Israel, and again speaking on behalf of the people to God. In these passages Moses reveals to the people the character of God, the results of obedience or disobedience to God's commandment, and how God acts in the life and history of his people. In several places Moses warned the people that if they obeyed God he would greatly bless them, but if they disobeyed him he would certainly punish them. In these passages Moses acted as a prophet of God, revealing to Israel God's true character. God's blessing would come to the whole nation and be seen in its life and history if it obeyed God: the nation would be strong and would defeat its enemies. On the other hand, if the nation disobeyed God, his punishment for sin would come upon the nation and be seen in its history; if the nation grew weak and was invaded, then God was punishing it. It is this way of presenting Old Testament history that is seen in the books collectively referred to as the Former Prophets. The style, or interpretation, of history is a reflection of what Moses said in the Book of Deuteronomy, and hence it is called the "Deuteronomic" view of history. The facts are clearly illustrated in the Former Prophets, where the prophetic teaching of Moses about blessing and punishment is recorded. In the Book of Judges, for example, there is the record of a cycle of events: the people sin; God is angry and sells them into the hands of oppressors; during the oppression they cry to God for deliverance; God sends a judge, a warrior, and saves them, and the land enjoys peace again; at the death of the judge the people fall into sin again, and the cycle continues. Joshua's single failure at Ai, caused by Achan's covetousness, is a grim illustration of the same principle, that disobedience brings disaster.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: Give a brief survey of the books of Joshua and Judges as part of the Former Prophets.
idealAnswer: The book of Joshua deals with the history of Israel after the death of Moses, and with the conquest and settlement in the Promised Land. At every step Joshua was successful: the invasion of the land occupies chapters 1 to 5, the fall of Jericho chapter 6, the conquest of the south chapter 10, the conquest of the north chapters 11 and 12, the division of the land and the appointment of cities of refuge chapters 13 to 22, and the farewell address and death of Joshua chapters 23 and 24. The crossing of the Jordan, the capture of Jericho and the quick military operations against the important cities of Canaan all illustrate his successes. His one failure was at Ai, and the reason for the defeat was that Achan coveted some of the spoils from Jericho and kept them for himself instead of letting all be offered to God; he and his family suffered severe punishment in being totally destroyed. Here is a grim illustration of the prophetic interpretation of history, in which disobedience brings disaster. The one occasion when Joshua entered into a covenant with the people of Gibeon was described as a mistake, because Israel did not ask direction from the Lord. The second half of the book tells how the land was divided among the twelve tribes, and ends with the rededication of the people as Joshua renews the covenant at Shechem, where they cried, "The Lord our God we will serve, and his voice we will obey." Their spiritual enthusiasm did not last long, as the book of Judges shows. Judges covers the period between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel, roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C. It was a time of transition in which the only thing holding the scattered tribes together was their common faith: loyalty to God meant a strong united nation, while turning to the gods around brought weakness and division. The prophetic interpretation of this pattern is set out in Judges 2:11-23 in five stages, and the book ends with an appendix illustrating the moral and religious decline of the times, explained by the words, "There was no King in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes."

subject: OT
chapter: PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY
topic: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan
question: Describe the conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during Israel's settlement in the land of Canaan.
idealAnswer: The people who came from the desert with Moses came with their religion, Yahwism; the people in the land of Canaan had a religion, Baalism; and the question was what the relationship between the two religions was to be. Yahwism has a theological position of monolatry or henotheism, that is, worship was to be given exclusively to Yahweh. It abhors visual representation of any kind: the worship of Yahweh was very plain, with no statues or pictorial representation allowed. Yahwism laid no stress on sanctuaries or sacred places, for Yahweh is not the god of a particular place. It laid strong emphasis on morality and on keeping the commandments given at Mount Sinai; to worship Yahweh was primarily to keep his commandments. Baalism, by contrast, was a religion tied to the land, a religion of times and seasons. It was purely an agricultural religion that laid great emphasis on local shrines, sanctuaries and high places, and was intimately connected with the fertility of the land. It was polytheistic and laid no stress at all on morality; to worship Baal was to celebrate rites and festivals designed to procure the fertility of the land. The conflict arose from the settlement itself: the problem was how Israel could occupy the land without also taking over its religion. The Israelites were shepherds without very good ideas about food crop farming, the predominant occupation of the Canaanites, and since the Israelite was to sow crops it became necessary to adopt Baalism, which conflicted with the worship of Yahweh. The Canaanite neighbours told them that unless they adopted the worship of Baalism agricultural practice would be impossible. Another feature of Baalism was its festivals with their cultic practices, including orgies, feasting, drinking, eating and sex, so that from a purely sensory point of view Baalism was an attractive religion. The official theology was strict Yahwism, in which no compromises were accepted, and the Rechabites are an example of those who would not compromise at all. Generally, however, the relationship was one of compromise: Israel accepted that Yahweh could do all that Baal could do, and many of the words that applied to Baal were applied to Yahweh. Certain words, however, could not be applied to Yahweh: there was no way of thinking of him as dying and rising, or as one who approved of sexual expression in his worship.

topic: The Traditions of Elijah and Elisha
question: What do the traditions of Elijah and Elisha teach about the nature of prophetism in Israel in the 9th century B.C.?
idealAnswer: The accounts in 1 Kings 17 to 19 and in 2 Kings show that Elijah, who came from Tishbe in Gilead, prophesied during the reign of Ahab, about 873 to 851 B.C., while Elisha's ministry ran from the period of Ahab through to the reign of Jehoahaz, about 815 to 800 B.C. The traditions of Elijah were basically concerned with the clash between Yahwism and Baalism. Elijah's prediction of drought in 1 Kings 17:1-5, the Mount Carmel contest in 1 Kings 18, the denunciation of the crime against Naboth in 1 Kings 21 and his oracles against Ahaziah in 2 Kings 1 are all examples of his handling of that conflict. Elisha's traditions, however, do not show the same tension between Yahwism and Baalism, but rather the performance of signs and wonders both at personal and at national levels, as recorded in 2 Kings chapters 2 to 8. The traditions of the two men are therefore of vital importance for understanding the nature of prophetism in Israel in the ninth century B.C. The Elijah tradition, and especially the Mount Carmel contest, illustrates the variety of prophetism in that century. Though Elijah had connections with the prophetic communities, he was pre-eminently solitary: he travelled alone, sometimes vanished mysteriously and then reappeared unheralded, and this tradition is of peculiar importance. Elisha's performance of signs and wonders was meant to demonstrate the power of Yahweh and to issue a call to serve him alone. Taken together, these traditions show that in the ninth century B.C. Israel had individual prophets as well as prophetic groups.

subject: OT
topic: Socio-Economic Situation
question: Describe the socio-economic situation in Israel during the ministry of Amos.
idealAnswer: The military success of Jeroboam II brought with it improved economic development. Israel at this time built a close relationship with Phoenicia, which remained the dominant commercial power in the Middle East. Among the economic policies of Jeroboam were the imposition of tolls upon all caravans passing through Israel, which brought a lot of revenue to the treasury; increased opportunities for international trade; and the development of Samaria into a strong commercial centre. The splendid buildings erected by Jeroboam II in Samaria demonstrated well enough the prosperity of the northern state, and many people became very rich as a result of the increased opportunities for international trade. One important feature of the period, however, was that the rich became richer while the poor became poorer, and it is noteworthy how repeatedly Amos attacked this division between the rich and the poor. He attacked especially the luxury of the rich as against the misery of the poor. Amos gives a clear picture of the circumstances of the time: he speaks of the many fine buildings in the capital, Samaria, and of the fact that those who owned such buildings, the rich merchants and others, had one aim, to increase their profit no matter the means. Amos stated that these merchants hated the day in which they could not do any business. These rich men were supported by their wives, who demanded more and more luxury. While the houses of the rich were loaded with goods and other luxurious items, the poor were subjected to a cruel economic exploitation. Small businessmen were forced out of business by the big monopolies, without any possibility of redress at the courts. Justice was perverted by the judges, who took bribes, and the justice offered to the poor was a bitter pill. The legal process had been totally corrupted and was used as an instrument of oppression; the courts had become little more than a market where the poor man was enslaved and his rights totally violated.

Close relationship with Phoenicia, the dominant commercial power of the Middle East

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Amos
question: Discuss the message of the prophet Amos.
idealAnswer: Amos' message is dominated by the idea of God's righteousness, and the essence of his teaching is found in Amos 5:24. In the Old Testament the word righteousness belongs to the vocabulary of salvation. When it is used of God it refers to God keeping his promises, being just to his people and persevering in his love towards them. Righteousness is a covenant word, and the righteousness of God refers to his faithfulness in keeping his covenant. When the word is used of people it means their faithfulness in keeping the covenant: they keep their promises and respond to God in love and faith, while towards their neighbour a righteous man is compassionate, kind and charitable. In the Old Testament righteousness is not a legal but a moral and spiritual concept, and its opposite is the wicked man, who is cruel, selfish, greedy and hateful. By righteousness Amos means the goodness of God expressed for the people's salvation, and he condemns the people because they have failed to respond to God with righteousness themselves. First, he condemned their unrighteousness, which is the exploitation of the poor and the denial of human rights. He was particularly concerned with the administration of justice at the law courts, for he believed the courts should represent the central institution of the nation's life, since it is there that righteousness should be revealed and justice established. The courts should defend the weak and the poor, but instead the justice given to the poor was as bitter as wormwood and the legal processes were used as instruments of oppression. He also condemned the affluence of the wealthy classes, because their wealth had been gained by the oppression of the poor. Secondly, he condemned their religion, which was without righteousness. The people worshipped Yahweh, but Amos condemned this because one cannot worship Yahweh without righteousness. Their religion was full of rituals but empty in content, and God had no time for ritualistic religion without righteousness: true religion must be demonstrated in terms of compassion and social justice. Thirdly, Amos asserted that God's punishment was coming upon the people for their lack of righteousness. The punishment would include exile, political and military defeat and the destruction of the nation; judgment was already at the door, and like a lion ready to spring on its prey so Yahweh was ready to judge his people.
keyPoints: The message is dominated by the righteousness of God; its essence is Amos 5:24
Righteousness belongs to the vocabulary of salvation and is a covenant word
Used of God it means faithfulness in keeping his covenant; used of people, faithfulness to it
Righteousness is not a legal but a moral and spiritual concept

Special concern with the corruption of the law courts and the affluence gained by oppression
Second charge: religion without righteousness — full of ritual but empty in content

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: Give an account of the five visions of doom in the Book of Amos.
idealAnswer: The first vision is the plague of locusts in Amos 7:1-3. God revealed to Amos in a vision that the crops were to be destroyed by an invasion of locusts; Amos interceded for Israel and the destruction did not take place. The second is the vision of fire in Amos 7:4-6. Amos saw a destructive fire which dried up all the waters of Palestine and which was to fall upon the land to punish sin; again the prophet pleaded for mercy, and again God set aside this deserved punishment. The third is the vision of the plumb line in Amos 7:7-16, in which Amos saw the Lord measuring a wall with a plumb line to find out whether the wall was straight. God informed Amos that he would continue to test Israel with the plumb line of heavenly justice, that he would no longer turn away from punishing them, and that he would destroy the dynasty of Jeroboam II by the sword. This really occurred: Jeroboam II was succeeded by his son Zechariah, who was assassinated after a reign of only six months. God later used the same plumb line on Judah during the reign of King Manasseh. The fourth is the vision of the basket of summer fruit in Amos 8:1-14. The Lord showed Amos a basket filled with ripe fruit and explained that it symbolised Israel, which was now ripe for judgment. The cruel and materialistic merchants of the northern kingdom had robbed the poor by selling them mouldy food and had trampled upon the needy; they longed for the Sabbath and the religious holidays to be over so that they might start cheating again with weighted scales and undersized measures; and they made slaves of the poor, buying them for a piece of silver or a pair of shoes. When judgment came, singing in the temple would be turned to weeping, dead bodies would be scattered everywhere, fearful heavenly signs would occur, and there would be no comforting words from God. The fifth is the vision of the Lord at the altar in Amos 9:1-10. In this final vision Amos saw the Lord at the altar speaking of the final destruction of Israel. The destruction of the nation would be pursued relentlessly, and the Lord would track down and overtake all who tried to escape. This last vision was frightening because the Lord himself entered the scene.
keyPoints: First vision: the plague of locusts (7:1-3), averted by the prophet's intercession
Second vision: the destructive fire (7:4-6), also set aside when Amos pleaded for mercy

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
question: Outline the evidence for dating the ministry of the prophet Malachi.
idealAnswer: The exact time of Malachi's ministry is not given, but there are important indications which put the date of the book sometime after the return from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem, during the period of Ezra and Nehemiah. First, the prophet must have prophesied after the exile because he mentions a governor as being over the land in 1:8. This was a political condition which existed when the Jews returned from Babylon; before the exile the political leader of the nation was a king. Haggai used the word governor to describe Zerubbabel. Secondly, he must have prophesied after the ministry of Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied during the time of the building of the temple, from 520 to 516 B.C. This is because there is no reference in Malachi to the rebuilding of the temple, and the impression of a drift into a casual attitude regarding worship shows that some time had passed since the rebuilding took place. Temple services had been resumed long enough for the priests to become weary with the regular performance of them, and some irregularities had crept in. Thirdly, there are details which link the prophet to the time of Nehemiah, especially during the latter years of his governorship over Judah. Nehemiah came to Jerusalem to be governor in 445 B.C. He served in that capacity for some years and then returned temporarily to Persia in 433 B.C. After his return to Jerusalem he found gross sin and violation of the Law, as recorded in Nehemiah 13. There is a very close agreement between Nehemiah 13 and the Book of Malachi, and so we can infer that Malachi prophesied during the return of Nehemiah, probably a few years after 433 B.C. Malachi is the last prophet of the Old Testament, and his book ends the Old Testament revelation; there follow four hundred years of silence, after which John the Baptist appeared to prepare the way for the Messiah.

subject: OT
topic: The nature of His Message
question: What are the six charges which Malachi brings against the nation of Israel?
idealAnswer: The theme of the Book of Malachi is "God's Rebuke of Israel's Outrageous Sins", and this theme is developed into six charges against the nation. The first is that Israel has doubted God's love, in Malachi 1:1-15. God reminds the people of his great love for them, but they complain, "How have you loved us?" and he answers by referring Israel to its own history: "Is not Esau Jacob's brother? Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated." The second is that Israel has despised God's name, in 1:6 to 2:9. The word name refers not to a proper name or title but to God's person, to who he is; and the priests despised it by placing defiled food upon his altar and offering blind, crippled or diseased animals, when the Law of Moses taught that only the best should be brought. The third is that Israel has defied God's law, in 2:10-16. The people had defied the law forbidding mixed marriages, marrying the daughters of a strange god, which was forbidden on religious and not on racial grounds; and they had defied God's original intention against divorce, so that God says plainly, "I hate divorce." The fourth is that Israel has disdained God's justice, in 2:17 to 3:6. The Jews of Malachi's day struggled with the problem of why the wicked apparently prosper while the righteous suffer, forgetting that God is long suffering and that he has a timetable for his judgment. The fifth is that Israel has disregarded God's tithes, in 3:7-12. Tithing was God's way of providing the means to sustain his work and provide for his ministers, and by withholding the tithe the people were robbing God. The sixth is that Israel has discredited God's service, in 3:13 to 4:6. The majority said that it does not pay to serve the Lord, complaining that God had not rewarded their religion, but a remnant believed that it does pay to serve the Lord, and of these a book of remembrance was written before him.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: Explain how Israel had disregarded God's tithes, and state what Malachi required of the people.
idealAnswer: The Hebrew word for tithe is ma'aser, and it means a tenth. Its origin is difficult to trace, but it is known to have existed in Babylon in ancient times, and also in Persia, Egypt and China. It is quite certain that Abraham knew of it when he migrated from Ur, and since Melchizedek was a priest of the Most High it is certain that in Abraham's day the giving of tithes had been recognised as a holy deed. It is recorded in Genesis 28:16-22 that when Jacob made his covenant with God at Bethel the payment of tithe was included. The legal requirement of tithing developed late, and so the customs of its payment varied. At first the one who paid the tithe was entitled to share it with the Levites, but after the Levitical code had been completed the tithes belonged exclusively to the Levites. If a Hebrew lived too far from the temple, he could sell his animals and use the money to buy substitutes there, a permission which eventually led to gross abuses by the priests. A penalty of twenty per cent of the tithe was exacted from anyone who sold his tithes and refused to use the money to pay for a substitute. Leviticus 27:30 makes it clear that a tithe of everything belonged to the Lord and was holy to him, and when the Levites received the tithe they in turn gave a tenth to provide for the priests. Tithing was God's way of providing the means to sustain his work and provide for his ministers, the priests. In Malachi's day there had been a total disregard for this rule. The people disobeyed the clear instructions of God's word on what was required, and hence they were robbing God; they were greedy and self-centred in spite of God's goodness to them. How long this had been going on we do not know, but the people were now experiencing God's chastisement and being deprived of his blessing. What should they do? The answer is simple. They must repent and bring the whole tithe into the storehouse. If they are willing to do this, God will open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing on them, and he will also remove the chastisement they were experiencing in their agriculture.
